analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal statutory right to obtain and provide contraception, overriding state restrictions.
analysis.headline: The Senate fell 9 votes short of the 60 needed to open debate on the Right to Contraception Act, failing 51–39, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write contraception into federal law as a right: individuals could obtain contraceptives — pills, IUDs, emergency contraception, sterilization, fertility-awareness methods — and doctors, nurses, and pharmacists could provide them, even in states that try to restrict or ban them. It would override state limits on contraception and let the Attorney General, patients, and providers sue in federal court to strike down restrictions, with attorney's fees for those who win. It does not change what health insurance must cover, so it addresses government restrictions, not cost.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use or may use contraception — most women and many men at some point in their lives — especially those in states that have moved to restrict access to IUDs, emergency contraception, or sterilization. Health care providers, including pharmacists, nurses, and doctors, also gain a federal defense if state law penalizes them for providing contraception or related information.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an explicit federal right for individuals to obtain contraceptives and engage in contraception, and a matching right for health care providers — including pharmacists, nurses, and nurse practitioners — to provide contraceptives and contraception-related information, free from state limits [S2].

Overrides state laws that restrict the sale, provision, or use of contraceptives, and applies even over the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, so a state could not invoke religious-objection law to block access [S2].

Gives real enforcement teeth: the Attorney General can sue states that violate the right, and patients and providers can sue directly in federal court, with injunctions available and attorney's fees awarded to prevailing plaintiffs [S2].

Sponsors framed the goal as protecting access before it is lost, citing the Supreme Court's 2022 decision overturning Roe v. Wade and Justice Thomas's suggestion that the Court could revisit the constitutional right to contraception [S2].

analysis.who_pays: State governments that restrict or want to restrict contraception would lose that authority and face federal lawsuits. The bill would also generate litigation costs, since private plaintiffs get attorney's fees from prevailing, and states lose immunity from these suits in federal court. Taxpayers fund the enforcement, though the bill carries no direct spending.

drawbacks.text: The preemption is unusually broad: it supersedes any state or federal law, common law included, 'notwithstanding' the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which critics said sweeps well beyond codifying past practice and could override state conscience protections and health regulations [S2].

It does nothing about price. The bill explicitly leaves health insurance coverage law untouched, so a person protected from a state ban could still face out-of-pocket costs for the same contraceptive [S2].

The definition of contraception includes sterilization procedures, and while the bill requires voluntary, informed consent, opponents argued that inclusion, combined with the private right of action and the stripping of state immunity, invites litigation against states and officials [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and direct: a legal backstop for the roughly half the population that uses contraception at some point, and for the providers who serve them, in a period when several states have moved to restrict certain methods. The fiscal cost is minimal. The real cost is to state regulatory authority, and the bill's preemption is written aggressively — it deliberately overrides religious-objection law and strips state immunity — which is exactly what opponents attacked and why it could not attract anywhere near the 60 votes needed. An honest supporter would also concede the bill leaves the affordability problem untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It failed a Senate procedural vote — 51 senators voted to open debate on the bill, but 60 were needed — and the Senate then tabled the motion to proceed, killing it for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on May 21, 2024, with 50 cosponsors — 47 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and 3 of its 4 Independents — and it was placed directly on the Senate calendar [S3][S4].
Majority Leader Schumer moved to proceed to the bill and filed cloture, the step that requires 60 senators to cut off debate before the Senate can even begin considering a bill [S4].

On June 5, 2024, cloture on the motion to proceed failed 51–39: 46 of 47 voting Democrats and all 3 voting Independents voted yes, while 38 of 40 voting Republicans voted no; only Senators Collins and Murkowski crossed party lines to support it [S5].
The Senate then agreed by voice vote to table the motion to proceed, and no further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments that restrict contraception kept full authority over access, and the senators who opposed the bill avoided a direct recorded vote on the substance, having blocked it at the procedural stage. No one gained a contraception right.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States restricting contraception; senators who blocked it

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost entirely by party: 46 of 47 voting Democrats and all 3 voting Independents supported opening debate, 38 of 40 voting Republicans opposed it, and only Senators Collins and Murkowski crossed over — a 51–39 result against a 60-vote threshold.

industries.note: The bill bars states from restricting the sale or use of any FDA-approved contraceptive, protecting and potentially enlarging the market for these products. Its interest runs alongside users' interest in access. [S2]
Pharmacists are named among the protected providers, giving them a federal defense if state law penalizes dispensing contraception. [S2]
The bill deliberately excludes insurance coverage law, so insurers face no new mandates — but that also means the bill does nothing about what contraceptives cost patients out of pocket. [S2]
States that restrict contraception would lose that authority entirely and become subject to federal lawsuits from the Attorney General and private plaintiffs. [S2]
